United States, and yes, I do. I was involved in a bunch of "gifted" programs where I took the SATs in the 6th grade and again in the 8th to see how I was comparing with college bound seniors. In high school I took IT-PC support classes as well as AP Calc and learned how to build computers and do support work on them. On the other hand, it did nothing for my sister and the reason is that our parents got divorced when she was in preschool. Absolutely (USA). I was exposed to a broad range of topics and given good foundations upon which I built further education formally (university/grad school) and informally (learning through life). More importantly, I was taught how to think analytically and with an open mind.

It is worth mentioning that I went to private school. I understand that the public school experience is very different. A good education is available in many places, but not with the attention and dedication that was provided at my school.
I'm mostly interested in finding out what people think works and what people think doesn't work. What do you think made your school so effective?

Low student to teacher ratio. Highly educated teachers. Teachers were minimally influenced in their curricula by administrators (they had to cover certain minimums, but how they accomplished that was up to them). Once I got to high school, teachers that were highly over qualified for their jobs (meaning they had the opportunity to make way more money elsewhere, but decided to teach instead). Excellent resources. Highly motivated student body, and parents that were attentive and involved with their children's education (hugely important in my opinion).

I have friends that are teachers now, and they say that the most sought after job in the area is teaching at the school that I went to. Having their pick of the best teachers must be a big help.
You are a very lucky duck. Just know that.

It's kind of a double edged sword. I went to a private catholic school for K-6. Without it, I don't think I would've developed as well academically and gotten the degree/career/job/life I have. On the other hand, the kids were all kind of rich and snobby, and I didn't make really any friends, even developed some bad social habits. Coupled with having no kids my age in the neighborhood, I really had no social outlet. When I finally got into public school, I wasn't really prepared for interacting with new crowds and making friends. It got better in High School, and I had a small, dedicated group of friends, but all my social problems didn't get fully resolved till about 21. I know the grass isn't always greener, but I always wondered if I had started in public schools if I could have actually made more friends, became better adjusted, and have somewhat of a happy childhood.

The actual knowledge I gained during K-12, outside of mathematics, is not really relevant to my day to day life. The actual process of learning has been much more beneficial in that I figured out by what methods I learn best. That foundation is what has allowed me to get to where I am today.

I think it also helped by putting me in a social atmosphere surrounded by my peers. Without those interactions, my social skills would not have developed to what they are now. However, this could also be true for those that did not attend school.

What's the weather like?

Would you recommend Taiwan for a vacation?

As of now, it's really hot and humid. The typhoon just passed, so sun is finally shining. If you're into beaches, definitely stop by at the southern parts of Taiwan. If you like to eat, there's a ton to choose from at all major cities; if you're adventurous, you can try some of Taiwan's night markets.

I'm Canadian, but I'm sure North America's all one thing for receiving all that stuff called "made in Taiwan".

Do you get a sense, living in Taiwan, of what that means to the local world? Is there a sort of, "It's just a job but those suckers'll buy anything! mentality? Do Taiwanese people get to use any of that stuff? Does it just disappear onto big ships?

It's one thing over here to find that mark on so much different merchandise. What does that mean, in Taiwan? I have this image of a gray, grimy world with alleys full of welding sparks and the smell of hot plastic....

From a manufacturing stand point, I think Taiwan locals are proud that they provide better working conditions than... let's say... China. As for the mentality, I'm leaning towards that a majority of them just want to make quick money, but I definitely seen a fair share of local who pride themselves on the products they put out such as Giant Bicycle.
How do you feel about tensions with the PRC? Given as Taiwan is technically the Republic of China, do you get any sense that Taiwan has any inclination to recover the mainland?

I can't really comment on how I feel. However, I definitely see a huge perspective differences between the young and older generation of Taiwan locals on how they view Taiwan and China. The younger generation are clamoring for independence and to be treated as an independent country, while the older generation wants to be part of China. I'm pretty sure it's much more complicated than that, but it's definitely a sight to behold.

When you mean "part of China" do you mean part of the PRC or is it more of a harkening to the political stance of Taiwan as being the Republic of China? If not, does anyone at all buy into the idea of the RoC being the legitimate government of China as a whole.

As for your own feelings (or at least the zeitgeist) are you worried about PRC aggression at all or does it more feel like empty political posturing?

It's more of a political stance of Taiwan.

To be honest, I haven't sensed any PRC aggression at all from the locals or the media, so I'm not too worried at all.
